pos: n. (one who sleeps; a man asleep when he should be awake)
etymology: Saxon slaepere, from slaepan, to sleep. In Jonah 1:6 it renders a Hebrew participle of radam, to be in a deep or heavy sleep.
biblical_def: The ship is breaking up, the mariners have thrown the cargo overboard, every heathen sailor is crying to his god — and the prophet of the LORD is below deck, asleep. The shipmaster finds him there: “What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not” (Jonah 1:6). It is one of the sharpest rebukes in Scripture, and it comes from a pagan sailor to a prophet. The Hebrew word is the heavy sleep of Adam under God's hand and of Sisera under Jael's; it is not a nap but a stupor. Jonah had fled the word of the LORD, and flight from God ends in insensibility. The Authorized Version uses sleeper once, and the apostle gives it a wider application: “Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light” (Ephesians 5:14). Spiritual sleep is the condition of the unregenerate and the besetting danger of the believer who has run from a duty. The men who did not know God were praying; the man who knew Him was unconscious. That is what disobedience does to a soul.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SLEEPER, noun One that sleeps; a lazy, inactive person; also, a horizontal timber supporting others.
webster_full: SLEEPER, noun One that sleeps; a lazy, inactive person.
2. That which lies dormant, as a law not executed.
3. An animal that lies dormant in winter, as the bear.
4. In building, a piece of timber lying on or near the ground to support joists or other timbers.
5. In New England, one of the pieces of timber laid across the sills on which the floor is laid.
scriptures: Jon 1:6
What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not.
Jon 1:5
But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep.
Eph 5:14
Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.
corruption_summary: Spiritual sleep is now described as burnout or a dry season; Scripture calls the sleeper to arise and call upon God.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic register has a gentler vocabulary for Jonah's condition: he was exhausted, he was in a season of depletion, he needed rest. The text gives no such account. He was in flight from the word of the LORD, and the sleep was the fruit of the flight. Naming it fatigue removes the only thing that could have helped him, which is the shipmaster's command to arise and pray.

The principle to recover is that a heathen may rebuke a prophet, and the rebuke may be right. The mariners prayed; Jonah slept. When unbelievers are more in earnest about perishing than a believer is, the believer is the one asleep, and Ephesians 5:14 is addressed to him.

pos: n. pl. (men armed with the sling; stone-throwers in war)
etymology: From sling, Saxon slingan, to throw or cast. In 2 Kings 3:25 it renders a Hebrew participle of qala', to sling or hurl.
biblical_def: When the allied armies have broken every city of Moab and come at last to Kirharaseth, one force keeps working: “only in Kirharaseth left they the stones thereof; howbeit the slingers went about it, and smote it” (2 Kings 3:25). The slingers are the light infantry of the ancient East, and Scripture takes them seriously. Benjamin bred them — “armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow” (1 Chronicles 12:2) — and Judges records seven hundred Benjamite left-handers who could sling at a hair and not miss. The sling is the weapon of the man who has no armour, and it is therefore the weapon of the shepherd. David came against Goliath with five stones and a sling, and the Philistine fell. The Authorized Version uses slingers once, in this plural and military sense. The entry belongs beside sling: the thing is small, cheap, and in a practised hand decisive, which is exactly how God chooses to win. He does not need the smith, the forge, or the chariot. A stone and a steady arm will do when the LORD has given the word.

webster_full: SLINGER, noun One who slings or uses a sling.

2. A throw; a stroke.
3. A kind of hanging bandage for a wounded limb.

scriptures: howbeit the slingers went about it, and smote it.

So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and smote the Philistine, and slew him; but there was no sword in the hand of David.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The only misuse to name is the sentimental one that turns David's sling into a lesson about self-belief. The text says the opposite: there was no sword in the hand of David, and he told Goliath the battle was the LORD's. The weapon is mentioned precisely because it was inadequate.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is not served by superior equipment. Israel had no smith in Saul's day and still had slingers; the Benjamites practised with both hands; and the LORD gave victories through men who carried stones.

pos: n. pl. (archers; those who shoot from a wall or a bow)
etymology: From shoot, Saxon sceotan, to dart or let fly. In 2 Samuel 11:24 it renders a Hebrew participle of yarah, to shoot or cast.
biblical_def: Joab's messenger reports from Rabbah: “And the shooters shot from off the wall upon thy servants; and some of the king's servants be dead, and thy servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also” (2 Samuel 11:24). The sentence is constructed to bury one name in a casualty list, and David knows it, because David wrote the order. The archers on the wall were real, the losses were real, and the whole arrangement was a murder dressed as a battle report. David's answer is the most chilling line in the chapter: “Let not this thing displease thee, for the sword devoureth one as well as another” (2 Samuel 11:25). He blames the sword. He consoles the general. He takes the widow. The Authorized Version prints shooters here, where the margin of 1 Samuel 31:3 also offers it for the archers who wounded Saul. The dictionary notes the grim symmetry: the shooters on the wall at Rabbah served a king's adultery, and the shooters at Gilboa ended a king's reign. Psalm 51 is the only honest sequel to this verse, and it is David's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SHOOTER, noun One that shoots; an archer; a gunner.
webster_full: SHOOTER, noun One that shoots; an archer; a gunner.
SHOOT, verb transitive To let fly and drive with force; as, to shoot an arrow.
2. To discharge and cause to be driven with violence; as, to shoot a ball.
3. To send out; to push forth; as, a plant shoots a branch.
SHOOT, verb intransitive To be emitted, sent or driven along.
scriptures: And the shooters shot from off the wall upon thy servants; and some of the king's servants be dead, and thy servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.
Let not this thing displease thee, for the sword devoureth one as well as another: make thy battle more strong against the city, and overthrow it: and encourage thou him.
Psa 51:4
Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest.
corruption_summary: David's sin is often handled as a lapse or a failure of leadership; Scripture calls it murder and adultery, confessed as such.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions meet here. The first excuses David by his office or his era — a king's prerogative, an ancient custom, a moment of weakness. Scripture records a conspiracy to kill a faithful soldier so the king could keep the soldier's wife, and Nathan names it plainly: thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword.

The second corruption is despair — the assumption that such a man is beyond grace. Psalm 51 refuses both. David calls it evil in God's sight, pleads nothing but mercy, and is forgiven without the sin being minimised. That is the Reformed doctrine of repentance in one psalm.

pos: n. (one who moves or stirs up; an instigator)
etymology: From move, Latin movere, to stir. In Acts 24:5 it renders the Greek kinounta, from kineo, to set in motion.
biblical_def: Tertullus opens the prosecution before Felix with a charge of sedition: “For we have found this man a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes” (Acts 24:5). Three accusations in one breath — plague, agitator, cult leader — and not one of them touches doctrine. The strategy is ancient and current: when a man cannot be refuted, have him charged with disturbing the peace. Paul's reply refuses the frame and goes straight to the thing actually at issue: “But this I confess unto thee, that after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets” (Acts 24:14). He will not plead that he is harmless. He pleads that he is orthodox — that what they call heresy is the faith of the fathers and the plain sense of the Scriptures. The Authorized Version uses mover once, in this accusation. A faithful minister will be called a mover of sedition, because the gospel does in fact overturn things; what he must never be is guilty of the charge as laid.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): MOVER, noun One that moves; one that gives motion; a proposer; an instigator.
webster_full: MOVER, noun A person or thing that gives motion, or impels to action.
2. He that moves, or offers a proposition; a proposer.
3. One that stirs up or excites; an instigator.
4. A proposer in a deliberative assembly.
MOVE, verb transitive To impel; to carry, convey or draw from one place to another.
scriptures: Act 24:5
For we have found this man a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes:
But this I confess unto thee, that after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets:
Act 17:6
These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also;
corruption_summary: The charge of disturbing the peace is still the preferred weapon against preaching that cannot be answered on its merits.
corruption_paragraphs: Tertullus did not argue that Paul was wrong. He argued that Paul was trouble. The same substitution operates whenever doctrine is answered with a complaint about tone, divisiveness, or harm — the question of truth is replaced by the question of disturbance, and the accused is required to prove himself inoffensive rather than faithful.

The principle to recover is Paul's refusal. He did not defend his manner; he confessed his creed, grounded it in the law and the prophets, and let the charge stand or fall against it. Acts 17:6 shows the accusation was in one sense accurate: the gospel does turn the world upside down.

pos: n. (one who receives; here, the officer who collects tribute)
etymology: From receive, Latin recipere, to take back. In Isaiah 33:18 it renders the Hebrew shoqel, the weigher — the man who weighed out the tribute silver.
biblical_def: Isaiah describes Jerusalem looking back on the Assyrian terror after it has passed: “Thine heart shall meditate terror. Where is the scribe? where is the receiver? where is he that counted the towers?” (Isaiah 33:18). Three officers of the occupying power are named and all three are gone. The scribe kept the list; the receiver weighed the silver; the counter of towers surveyed the walls for the siege. Hezekiah had stripped the temple to pay such a receiver (2 Kings 18:15-16), and the terror of those years was the sound of weights in a scale. Now the apostrophe is empty — nobody answers, because nobody is there. And the reason is given four verses later: “For the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us” (Isaiah 33:22). The dictionary reads this as the ordinary pattern of providence. The tribute-weigher of an empire looks permanent while he is weighing. He is not. The office that remains is the LORD's threefold office — judge, lawgiver, king — and Isaiah sets it exactly where the Assyrian bureaucracy used to stand.

webster_full: RECEIVER, noun One who takes or receives.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The misreading to name is the political one, which treats Isaiah 33 as a nationalist taunt. Isaiah is not boasting about Judah; Judah had emptied the temple to pay the tribute. The whole weight of the passage rests on the LORD being judge, lawgiver, and king, not on Jerusalem being strong.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the impermanence of every office but God's. The receiver of tribute, the scribe, the surveyor of walls — each looked like the fixed order of the world, and Isaiah asks where they are.

pos: n. (one who takes; in Isaiah 24:2, the taker of usury)
etymology: From take, Saxon tacan, to seize or receive. In Isaiah 24:2 it stands in the phrase the taker of usury, Hebrew nosheh, the exactor of interest.
biblical_def: Isaiah's picture of universal judgment levels every rank in one verse: “And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him” (Isaiah 24:2). Six pairs, and in every pair the advantage is cancelled. The man who lent at interest and the man who paid it stand in the same ruin, because the thing that is coming is not an economic reversal but the LORD emptying the earth (Isaiah 24:1). The Authorized Version uses taker once, and it is worth noticing which pair the prophet put last. Usury — lending at interest to a poor brother — was forbidden in Israel: “thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury” (Exodus 22:25). The taker had the whip hand in every transaction. On the day Isaiah describes, he has nothing. The dictionary reads the verse as the end of all social leverage: in the final judgment no man is advantaged by his position, and the only question is whose he is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): TAKER, noun One that takes or receives; one that catches or apprehends.
webster_full: TAKER, noun One that takes or receives; one that catches or apprehends.

2. To lay hold on; to seize; to catch.
3. To receive with a certain disposition; as, to take a thing amiss.
4. To exact; as, to take usury.

Behold, the LORD maketh the earth empty, and maketh it waste, and turneth it upside down, and scattereth abroad the inhabitants thereof.
If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 24:2 is read as a levelling manifesto; it is a judgment oracle in which no rank survives, and rank is not the sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The liberationist reading takes this verse as a programme: the master and the servant made equal, the lender brought down to the borrower. That is not the prophet's point. The LORD is emptying the earth, and the pairs are listed to show that judgment is no respecter of station. Isaiah does not abolish the master; he announces that the master will stand under the same wrath.

The principle to recover is that advantage does not transfer to the day of judgment. The taker of usury had leverage over the giver in every earthly transaction, and Exodus 22:25 had already told him it was unlawful against a poor brother. On the day Isaiah sees, the leverage is simply gone.

pos: n. pl. (farm implements with prongs; pitchforks)
etymology: Saxon forca, Latin furca, a fork. In 1 Samuel 13:21 it renders the Hebrew qilleshon, a three-pronged implement.
biblical_def: The Philistines had disarmed Israel by controlling the trade: “Now there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel: for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears” (1 Samuel 13:19). Israel therefore had to go down to the Philistines to have even its farm tools sharpened. The inventory is given: “Yet they had a file for the mattocks, and for the coulters, and for the forks, and for the axes, and to sharpen the goads” (1 Samuel 13:21). Forks here are the pronged implements of threshing and foddering, not table cutlery, which did not yet exist in England when the Authorized Version was made. The verse is a picture of a subject people: plough, mattock, axe, and fork are all they have, and even those must be edged by the enemy. The chapter ends with the famous summary — neither sword nor spear in any hand but Saul's and Jonathan's (1 Samuel 13:22). Then Jonathan climbs a cliff with his armourbearer and the LORD gives a victory. The dictionary notes the lesson the chapter is built to teach: Israel's weakness was real, humiliating, and no obstacle whatever to God.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The one genuine confusion is anachronism: readers picture table forks. The Hebrew is a three-pronged agricultural implement for threshing and foddering, and the verse is an inventory of a disarmed nation's farm tools, not its dinner service.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's people are often kept deliberately poor in means. Israel had no smith, and Jonathan still took the garrison at Michmash, for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few.

pos: n. (a steel tool with a roughened face, for sharpening or smoothing)
etymology: Saxon feol, a file. In 1 Samuel 13:21 it renders the Hebrew petsirah, from a root meaning to make blunt or to scrape — the margin reads a file with mouths.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses file once, and it is the most eloquent single word in a chapter about subjection: “Yet they had a file for the mattocks, and for the coulters, and for the forks, and for the axes, and to sharpen the goads” (1 Samuel 13:21). The Philistines permitted Israel no smith (1 Samuel 13:19). A nation with no forge has no swords, and a nation with no swords is a nation of farmers who must go down to their masters even to get an edge on a plough blade. Israel had one tool left — a file. The Hebrew is obscure and the translators put the literal sense in the margin, a file with mouths, meaning a rasp with cutting ridges. What matters theologically is the next verse: in the day of battle there was neither sword nor spear in any Israelite hand but the king's and his son's (1 Samuel 13:22). The narrative then gives Jonathan his victory at Michmash with no weapon worth naming. The file stands in Scripture as the measure of how little God requires in the hands of His people before He gives them the field.

pos: n. pl. (threads of drawn metal; here, gold cut into filaments)
etymology: Saxon wir, a thread of metal. In Exodus 39:3 it renders the Hebrew pathil, a thread or cord, used of the gold filaments beaten and cut for the ephod.
biblical_def: The workmanship of the high priest's ephod is described with unusual technical care: “And they did beat the gold into thin plates, and cut it into wires, to work it in the blue, and in the purple, and in the scarlet, and in the fine linen, with cunning work” (Exodus 39:3). Gold was hammered to leaf, the leaf cut into threads, and the gold thread woven in with the dyed yarns. Nothing in the tabernacle was improvised; every stitch was commanded, and this verse records obedience down to the metallurgy. The Authorized Version uses wires here alone. Two things follow. First, the garments of the priest were glorious by divine specification, not by the craftsmen's taste — Exodus 28 had given the pattern and Exodus 39 reports the execution. Second, the gold runs through the whole fabric: the priest who bore the names of Israel on his shoulders and breast was clothed in a weave that could not be separated from its gold. The dictionary reads the ephod typologically, as the great high priest's own glory and the names of His people worn into it, and declines to read it decoratively.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The misuse worth naming is aesthetic. The tabernacle's gold is sometimes offered as a warrant for ornament in Christian worship generally. The dictionary holds the regulative principle: what Scripture commands in corporate worship is required, and what it has not commanded is not permitted. The gold wires of the ephod were commanded in Exodus 28 and are not a precedent for what God has not commanded under the new covenant.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the exactness of obedience. Exodus 39 is a compliance report: they beat, they cut, they wove, as the LORD commanded Moses. Acceptable worship is specified worship.

pos: n. pl. (sockets or mountings in which stones are set)
etymology: From set, Saxon settan, to place. In Exodus 28:17 it renders the Hebrew millu'ah, a filling — the margin reads fill in it fillings of stone.
biblical_def: The breastplate of the high priest is built around twelve stones, and the stones must be held: “And thou shalt set in it settings of stones, even four rows of stones: the first row shall be a sardius, a topaz, and a carbuncle: this shall be the first row” (Exodus 28:17). The Hebrew is literally a filling — the hollow of the gold is filled with the stone — and the Authorized Version's margin preserves that sense. Three rows follow, ending “they shall be set in gold in their inclosings” (Exodus 28:20). Twelve stones, one for each tribe, each graven like a signet with a name, each held in its own socket of gold over the heart of the man who went in before God. The Authorized Version uses settings once. The typology is not subtle and the New Testament draws it out: the great High Priest bears the names of His people into the holy place, and none of them falls out of its setting. “They shall be mine, saith the LORD of hosts, in that day when I make up my jewels” (Malachi 3:17). A stone does not hold itself in gold; the gold holds the stone. That is the doctrine of preservation in a jeweller's word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SETTING, noun The act of setting; the act of sinking below the horizon; that in which something is set, as a gem.
webster_full: SETTING, noun The act of setting; the act of placing, fixing or establishing.
2. The act of sinking below the horizon; as the setting of the sun.
3. The act of becoming fixed or hard.
4. That in which something, as a precious stone, is set; the frame or socket.
SET, verb transitive To put or place; to fix in a certain position.
scriptures: And thou shalt set in it settings of stones, even four rows of stones: the first row shall be a sardius, a topaz, and a carbuncle: this shall be the first row.
And the fourth row a beryl, and an onyx, and a jasper: they shall be set in gold in their inclosings.
Mal 3:17
And they shall be mine, saith the LORD of hosts, in that day when I make up my jewels; and I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The one error to name is an old one: treating the stones of the breastplate as a system of correspondences — birthstones, lots, hidden meanings in the gems. Scripture gives the stones names and an order and says nothing of such a science. The meaning is plain on the face of the text: twelve names, over the heart, before the LORD continually.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is preservation. The stone is held by the gold, not by its own weight, and Malachi 3:17 says the LORD will make up His jewels and spare them. The saints are kept in their settings by the Priest who wears them.
